article.title: Life After Trump
article.author: Dick Price, Ken Levy
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The pre-Trump world is gone. But what replaces it? That was the central question posed by Ken Levy, LMFT, during his October 3 presentation, Life After Trump , at the 4th Annual Left Coast Forum at Cal State LA. Levy, a community-focused psychotherapist, longtime activist, and Coordinating Committee member of the Northeast LA Alliance for Democracy, challenged participants to look beyond the daily turbulence of the Trump presidency and confront a more fundamental problem: America cannot simply return to the political arrangements that made Trumpism possible. The session rejected two competing visions of America's future. One is the authoritarian agenda embodied in the Right's Project 2025. The other is the neoliberal Democratic Party's familiar promise to restore normalcy without fundamentally changing the political and economic arrangements that produced the crisis. Neither, Levy argued, offers an adequate path forward. Life After Trump: Rebuilding Democracy in a World That Cannot Go Back (53:25) The Old World Is Dying Levy began by invoking Italian political philosopher Antonio Gramsci's concept of an interregnum —a period when an old social order is collapsing but a new one has not yet emerged. Gramsci's frequently cited observation that the old world is dying while the new struggles to be born provided a framework for understanding the present political moment. Levy described Trumpism not as the creation of one individual but as the convergence of political movements that developed over decades. He identified an alliance involving white supremacists, Christian nationalists, economic elites, fossil-fuel interests, and wealthy technology entrepreneurs seeking to concentrate power and weaken democratic restraints. Project 2025, in his telling, represents far more than a collection of conservative policy proposals. It is part of a coordinated effort to transform government, dismantle institutional protections, and reverse social gains achieved during the twentieth century. Particularly troubling to Levy is the movement's apparent determination to consolidate power rather than treat electoral victories as temporary mandates subject to democratic accountability. He described the resulting political environment as one of orchestrated chaos: a continuous stream of actions, announcements, threats, and controversies that overwhelms the public's ability to respond. The consequences are psychological as well as political. People become exhausted. They lose their ability to distinguish immediate emergencies from long-term threats. Eventually, some retreat from political engagement altogether. For a psychotherapist concerned with community well-being, Levy sees that exhaustion as one of authoritarianism's most consequential effects. Related: Build a United Front against Fascism and a Workers Party Why Returning to Normal Is Not Enough If Levy rejected the Republican agenda, he was scarcely more enthusiastic about the Democratic Party establishment. He characterized the Biden administration's approach as an attempt to restore a previous political order rather than confront the systemic conditions that enabled Trump's rise. During the discussion, Levy pointed to the recurring Democratic tendency to avoid confronting past abuses in the name of moving forward. He also criticized Democratic leaders who, in his view, repeatedly prioritize political caution and accommodation over the demands of their own constituents. An audience member pressed him on whether a new generation of Democratic candidates could offer a meaningful alternative, or whether even self-described progressives would eventually accommodate existing power structures. Levy's response returned to a fundamental principle of organizing: the most important question is not simply what politicians promise, but what organized citizens can compel them to do. That distinction shifts the focus from finding an ideal candidate to building movements capable of holding elected officials accountable. It also requires acknowledging that political victories are rarely permanent. America's Long Struggle Between Democracy and Concentrated Power Levy situated the present crisis within a much longer American history. From abolition and Reconstruction to the labor movement and the New Deal, he described a recurring struggle between those seeking to broaden freedom and shared prosperity and those attempting to concentrate wealth, privilege, and political authority. Reconstruction offered an opportunity to remake the country following enslavement and the Civil War, but violent white supremacist resistance and political compromise undermined its promise. Labor organizations fought for economic dignity while corporate interests resisted their advances. The New Deal expanded the federal government's responsibility for economic security, only to face decades of organized opposition. For Levy, these historical examples demonstrate that social progress requires continuous organization and defense. The movements opposing that progress do not disappear after an election. They regroup, adapt, and develop new ways of exercising power. He extended that analysis to contemporary technology billionaires and intellectual figures associated with anti-democratic political ideas, including Peter Thiel and Curtis Yarvin. His concern was that the next generation of right-wing leadership could preserve Trumpism's authoritarian direction while adopting different methods and personalities. The danger, in other words, does not end when Trump leaves office. Related: Don't Obey in Advance: How Ordinary Americans Can Resist Authoritarianism From Passive Consumers to Active Citizens Perhaps Levy's most important challenge was directed not at politicians but at the people attending his session. Modern American society, he argued, has conditioned people to think primarily as isolated individuals and consumers rather than members of a community with shared responsibilities. Economic pressure, cultural habits, and political alienation encourage people to concentrate on private survival. But democracy cannot function when citizens are reduced to spectators. Levy asked participants to consider what they wanted their lives and communities to become—and what they were prepared to contribute beyond their immediate personal interests. One participant expressed a desire simply to live without fear of government interference. Others discussed the difficulty of imagining a better future while political and economic circumstances seemed increasingly unstable. The conversation repeatedly returned to the idea of the common good. What do people owe one another? What responsibilities accompany citizenship? And how can individuals who feel powerless begin acting collectively? These questions transformed the gathering from a conventional political lecture into an invitation to rethink the relationship between personal responsibility and democratic action. Community as an Antidote to Authoritarianism The discussion ultimately turned toward the importance of rebuilding community. One participant observed that meaningful change would require moving from a culture organized around individual advancement toward one in which people again understand themselves as part of a collective. Levy agreed, emphasizing that isolation makes people more vulnerable to fear, exhaustion, and political withdrawal. Community offers something different: companionship, mutual support, shared purpose, and the possibility of effective collective action. He pointed to demonstrations and organizing efforts that bring people together not simply to oppose particular policies but to experience solidarity. Protests, he suggested, can be occasions of connection and even joy, reminding participants that they are not facing political threats alone. This, he explained, was one of the reasons for creating the Left Coast Forum. The gathering was intended not only to expose participants to new ideas but also to help organizers, activists, and community members find one another and develop relationships capable of sustaining future work. Levy stressed that meaningful action need not begin on a grand scale. Writing letters, contacting representatives, supporting organizations, attending demonstrations, contributing resources, and participating in local campaigns are all ways of developing political power. What matters is connecting those individual efforts to broader collective movements. Related: Nina Turner: There Is No Economic Justice Without Racial Justice. The Future Is Something We Must Build Life After Trump did not end with a detailed blueprint for a post-Trump society. That was deliberate. Levy's session was conceived as a conversation in which participants could begin identifying their own priorities and responsibilities rather than passively receiving a prescribed program. The discussion exposed the difficulty of imagining alternatives when so much political energy is consumed by resisting immediate threats. But it also suggested a starting point. A post-Trump agenda must address more than the conduct of one president. It must confront the concentration of economic and political power, defend multiracial democracy, restore the principle of the common good, and create durable organizations capable of demanding accountability. The challenge is not merely to defeat an authoritarian movement or elect a different set of political leaders. It is to build a society in which ordinary people possess the collective power to determine their own future. And that work, Levy reminded his audience, begins long before the next election.
